docs.title: Information and Decision Sciences (IDS) PhD Program
docs.text:
Welcome. This site is a supplemental resource for prospective students exploring the PhD program in Information and Decision Sciences at the Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota.

The Information and Decision Sciences (IDS) PhD trains researchers who study how individuals, organizations, and technology intersect — drawing on computer science, economics, organizational behavior, and behavioral science. The University of Minnesota established one of the first doctoral programs in management information systems in the United States, and the Information and Decision Sciences department remains among the top-ranked programs worldwide.

This is not an official Carlson School or University of Minnesota website

This page is maintained by the Information and Decision Sciences PhD Coordinator to answer questions that come up often from prospective applicants, in plain language. It does not set policy, and it does not replace or override official Carlson School or University of Minnesota sources. Where facts can change — requirements, deadlines, funding, faculty — this site links to the official page rather than restating the details, and the official page always governs.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
New to the program? Start with Considering the Information and Decision Sciences PhD? — it walks through what a research PhD is (and isn't), how to think about fit, what to prepare, and what to do before requesting a conversation with the program.

Need the official facts? Official Resources collects direct links to the Carlson School and University of Minnesota pages that govern admissions requirements, deadlines, and funding.

docs.title: About the Information and Decision Sciences department
docs.text:
Information and Decision Sciences faculty conduct research spanning artificial intelligence and machine learning, social networks and crowdsourcing, IT strategy, and human–computer/robot interaction, among other areas. The department is home to MIS Quarterly, a leading journal in the field, and hosts a weekly research seminar featuring visiting scholars. Graduates go on to research and teaching careers at universities worldwide.

For the authoritative, up-to-date description of the program, visit the official PhD in Information & Decision Sciences page.

docs.title: Considering the IDS PhD?
docs.text:
Prospective students often write to the department with a version of the same underlying question: "Is this kind of PhD right for me?" The official Carlson School pages answer what the program requires; this page tries to answer what the program is and how to think about fit, so that when you do reach out, we can have a more useful conversation.

This page is guidance, not policy. For requirements, deadlines, and funding, the Official Resources page links directly to the pages that govern those details.

docs.title: What is a research PhD — and what isn't it?
docs.text:
A PhD in Information and Decision Sciences is a research apprenticeship, not primarily an advanced professional credential. Over several years, you work closely with faculty to learn how to identify open research questions, design studies to address them, and communicate the results to a scholarly community. The degree exists to train independent researchers — most graduates go on to research- and teaching-focused faculty positions at universities.

This makes the Information and Decision Sciences PhD different in kind from professional graduate degrees such as an MBA or MSBA, which are designed to deepen a business or managerial career. If your primary goal is to advance more quickly within industry, add a technical or managerial credential to an existing career, or pivot into a new professional role, a professional master's program is very likely a better fit than a research PhD. If your goal is to spend the next several years learning to produce original scholarship — with the understanding that an academic research career, most often in a faculty position, is the typical outcome — the PhD path is worth exploring further.

docs.title: Program fit: research orientation, career goals, and preparation
docs.text:
A few questions can help you assess fit before you invest time in an application:

Research orientation. Are you drawn to open-ended questions that don't have a known answer yet, and comfortable with the slow, iterative pace of doing original research — including false starts and rejection along the way? Research training rewards curiosity and persistence more than it rewards prior mastery of a fixed body of professional knowledge.

Career goals. Would you be satisfied with an outcome centered on research and teaching, most typically at a university? The program is built around that goal; it is not primarily structured to accelerate an industry career, although some graduates do move into research-oriented industry roles.

Preparation. Strong quantitative and methodological preparation matters a great deal, because a large part of the coursework and the qualifying milestones involve rigorous methods training. The program draws on multiple reference disciplines — including computer science, economics, psychology, and organizational behavior — so there is no single required undergraduate major. What matters more is demonstrated ability to do rigorous, technical, or empirical work, and a genuine interest in the kinds of questions Information and Decision Sciences faculty study (information technology, decision-making, organizations, and their intersection).

Full-time commitment. The Information and Decision Sciences PhD is a full-time, in-residence program, not a part-time or remote course of study. Alongside coursework and research, students typically hold a combined teaching/research assistantship of up to an average of 20 hours per week. Students are expected to be present on campus, including over the summer for funded research. Plan on several years of sustained, full-time commitment to the program — matched by the program's commitment to you: admitted students are guaranteed five years of full funding as long as they remain in good academic standing (see Official Resources for current details).

docs.title: Nontraditional academic and professional backgrounds
docs.text:
Students enter Information and Decision Sciences PhD programs — and Information Systems PhD programs more broadly — from many academic and professional backgrounds, including computer science, engineering, mathematics, and business, and from prior careers in industry, law, consulting, or technology roles. A nontraditional path does not, by itself, disqualify you from being a strong candidate.

What matters most is not the label on your prior degree or job title, but:

  • a genuine and somewhat specific research interest — not just an interest in a topic, but curiosity about an open question related to it;
  • quantitative and methodological preparation sufficient to do rigorous research, or a credible plan to acquire it;
  • evidence of academic potential, such as strong academic records, research experience, or independent analytical work; and
  • a realistic understanding of what an academic research career involves, and genuine interest in that path specifically (rather than the PhD as a means to a different end).

If your background is nontraditional, it can help to address this directly and briefly in your application materials — connecting what you've done to the research questions you want to pursue — rather than assuming it will be read as a weakness.

docs.title: How to assess your research fit
docs.text:
The Information and Decision Sciences department admits students at the department level, not to work with one specific faculty member — so there is no need to secure an individual faculty member's agreement before applying. That said, thinking concretely about fit with the department's research strengths will make your application stronger and your own decision better informed.

Before reaching out to anyone in the program, we'd encourage you to:

  1. Review the Information and Decision Sciences faculty listing and read a handful of recent publications from two or three faculty members whose work looks interesting to you.
  2. Ask yourself whether you could articulate, in a paragraph, a research question you'd want to pursue and why it matters — not just a general topic area.
  3. Consider whether your quantitative and methodological background would let you contribute to that kind of work, or what you would need to add.

This kind of preparation is also exactly what a strong personal statement draws on, so the work is not wasted even before you apply.

docs.title: Can the program pre-assess my admission likelihood?
docs.text:
No. We are not able to assess your likelihood of admission from an informal email, a resume summary, or a short biography. Admission decisions are made at the department level — overseen by the Information and Decision Sciences PhD Coordinator together with several department faculty, not by any single faculty member — based on the complete application: academic records, standardized test scores, letters of recommendation, the personal statement, and overall research fit, evaluated against a competitive applicant pool each cycle. None of that can be reliably estimated from an introductory message, and we would rather not offer an impression that turns out to be misleading in either direction.

The most reliable way to gauge your own fit is to work through the Program fit and research fit sections above, and to review the official Admission Requirements & Deadlines page for the current, authoritative list of what the committee considers.

If, after that, you'd like a brief conversation about whether the program is a fit for you, email the Information and Decision Sciences PhD Coordinator at deliu@umn.edu with your CV and a short paragraph on your research interests and career goals — that's enough for us to have a useful conversation. This is a courtesy, not a required or formal part of the admissions process; every applicant is evaluated through the same complete-application process regardless of whether an earlier conversation took place. For factual questions instead — funding amounts, application logistics, deadlines — you don't need any of this; just ask directly (see Official Resources for the right contact).

docs.title: Cursor for doctoral work — more than a coding tool
docs.text:
Cursor is often introduced as an AI code editor — a place where software engineers ask an assistant to write, refactor, and explain code. That description is accurate, but incomplete. For doctoral students, the more useful way to think about it is as a research and workflow companion: an AI workspace that lives inside a real project folder and can sit next to the tools you already use for scholarship and day-to-day work.

What makes Cursor different from a chat window in a browser is context. You can open a dissertation chapter, a set of literature notes, a methods appendix, a GitHub repository, or a pile of Markdown files, and the assistant can see the structure of that work — not only the paragraph you pasted in. Used well, it becomes less like “ask a chatbot a question” and more like “work with a colleague who has read the folder.”

That matters in doctoral life because so much of the load is not a single writing task. It is staying oriented across a long project: remembering what a paper argued three months ago, turning messy notes into a coherent outline, keeping methods language consistent, preparing for a meeting, chasing an email thread, or regenerating an analysis table after the data change. Cursor is especially strong when those pieces live (or can be brought) into files the AI can actually work on — Markdown, LaTeX, code, CSV exports, research notes, and modern document systems connected through integrations.

docs.title: Where it helps doctoral work
docs.text:
Day-to-day ops. A surprising amount of PhD time is coordination: emails to coauthors, meeting prep, scheduling, finding the last version of a document, summarizing what was decided. With connectors to tools such as Gmail, Calendar, and Drive, Cursor can help draft messages, pull together a brief before a meeting, or locate related material without you leaving the workspace. One practical route for this is Composio: a single MCP connection that can unlock many apps (Google Workspace, Notion, Slack, GitHub, and others) and make them available inside Cursor, instead of wiring each tool separately.

Document and knowledge work. Doctoral writing is rarely linear. You revise a lit review while the theory section is still half-formed; you keep notes in Notion; you maintain chapter drafts in Markdown or Overleaf-style LaTeX; you collaborate through GitHub. Cursor is particularly good in Markdown- and GitHub-centered workflows, and it can help outline chapters, clean and reorganize notes, check consistency across sections, and turn fragmented annotations into something closer to a draft argument.

Treating a research library as a “knowledge codebase.” Software teams already treat a repository as the unit of collaboration. Researchers can do something similar: keep notes, memos, coded excerpts, outlines, and drafts in a project folder (or export / sync them there), then ask the assistant to search across that body of material — “where did we discuss construct validity?”, “summarize the themes in these policy notes,” “what gaps did I flag last month?” The quality of the help depends on how well your materials are organized, but the shift in mindset is useful even before the setup is perfect.

Coworking and iteration. Cursor works well as a back-and-forth partner: propose a structure, stress-test an argument, rephrase for academic tone, generate alternative outlines, or walk through reviewer comments point by point. The value is not that it “writes the dissertation for you.” The value is that it shortens the loop between stuck → draft → revise → next step.

Analysis and reproducibility (when you need it). If your work involves R, Python, notebooks, simulations, or data cleaning scripts, Cursor is still excellent at the job it was built for — writing and debugging code, explaining errors, and helping keep analysis, figures, and paper text in the same project so results stay reproducible.

You do not need to be a software engineer to benefit. Many of the highest-leverage uses for doctoral students are writing, synthesis, project organization, and workflow glue — with coding as an optional bonus when your methods require it.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. Install Cursor from cursor.com and create an account.
  2. Open a folder that already matters to you — a chapter draft, a notes directory, a paper project, or a small analysis repo — rather than starting from a blank chat.
  3. Try a concrete ask in the context of those files: outline the next section, reconcile two notes, explain a script, or propose a revision plan for a messy draft.
  4. When you are ready to go beyond local files, connect tools via MCP — either app-by-app (e.g. official Notion MCP) or through a multi-app layer such as Composio — using the resources below.

Student pricing note (as of mid-2026). The older “free year of Cursor Pro” student offer is closed to new claims. Anyone can start on the free Hobby plan via cursor.com/students. Watch that page for campus / online event promotions and whatever credit or discount paths Cursor currently lists for graduate students and researchers. Do not rely on older blog posts that still advertise a free Pro year — several widely shared guides are now out of date.

docs.title: Hook Cursor into day-to-day tools (MCP)
docs.text:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is how Cursor connects to external tools. Once set up, you can ask the agent to work against your real inbox, calendar, or Notion workspace — not only local files.

You can connect tools one at a time (official or community MCP servers), or use a multi-app connector. Composio is one of the easier options for the second path: authorize once, then expose many everyday apps to Cursor through a single MCP server (managed OAuth, tool discovery, and routing). That is often a better fit for doctoral workflows where you want Gmail + Calendar + Drive + Notion + Slack without maintaining a separate setup for each.

  • MCP for the non-engineer — clearest plain-language intro (Gmail, Calendar, Notion, and more)
  • Composio Connect docs — connect many apps to Cursor via one MCP endpoint
  • Composio in the Cursor marketplace
  • Notion MCP overview (official) — direct Notion ↔ Cursor path if you prefer not to go through a multi-app layer
  • Notion MCP setup with Cursor
  • Connect Gmail to Cursor via MCP — direct Gmail path; Composio is an alternative if you want Gmail plus other apps together

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Treat AI output as a draft and collaborator, not an authority — verify citations, methods claims, and factual claims against primary sources.
  • Follow your program’s and journals’ AI disclosure policies when using these tools for manuscripts, proposals, or coursework.
  • Prefer keeping sensitive data (human-subjects materials, unpublished peer review, credentials) out of cloud AI workflows unless you understand the tool’s data handling and your IRB / institutional rules.

docs.title: What you'll need to apply
docs.text:
A complete application typically includes:

  • A bachelor's degree (or equivalent) from an accredited institution
  • Transcripts of your undergraduate and/or graduate education
  • An official GMAT or GRE score
  • An official TOEFL or IELTS score (for international applicants)
  • A personal statement
  • Three letters of recommendation
  • A résumé/CV
  • The application fee

This is a general summary, not a checklist to apply against — score minimums, GPA guidance, and any other current specifics are set and maintained on the official Admission Requirements & Deadlines page.

docs.title: Key dates
docs.text:
• Application deadline: December 15 each year, for admission the following fall.
  • Admission decisions: made on a rolling basis starting in late January, with most decisions made in February–March, and all decisions finalized by April 15 (the national graduate-admissions response deadline).
  • Standardized test scores: must be no more than five years old as of your application date.

Exact dates (including any GMAT/GRE waiver-request deadline, which falls a few days before the application deadline) are set annually — always confirm against the official Admission Requirements & Deadlines and PhD FAQ pages.

docs.title: Program length
docs.text: The program is designed to be completed in about five years — matching the five years of guaranteed funding below — though the official FAQ notes that actual time to completion typically ranges four to six years. Coursework is concentrated in the first two years; the written preliminary exam typically follows in the summer after year two, and the oral preliminary exam typically in year three, ahead of dissertation research.

docs.title: Funding
docs.text:
All admitted students are guaranteed five years of full funding (tuition plus stipend, through a combination of teaching/research assistantships and fellowships), as long as they remain in good academic standing. For current stipend amounts and details, see the official page:

  • PhD Tuition & Aid — current funding, stipend, and tuition information.
